notes.definition: Ceramics (glass and clay ceramics), polymers and composites are materials whose properties depend on how they are made and on their structure. Composites combine a matrix (binder) with a reinforcement of fibres or fragments to give improved properties.
explanation: Glass and clay ceramics are both made by heating raw materials. Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone. Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass, so it is used for ovenware and laboratory glassware that must withstand heating. Clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made by shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace (a kiln). Ceramics are hard, brittle, have high melting points and are good electrical and thermal insulators.

The properties of polymers depend on what monomers they are made from and the conditions under which they are made. For example, low density poly(ethene) (LDPE) and high density poly(ethene) (HDPE) are both produced from ethene, but using different catalysts and reaction conditions. LDPE is made at very high pressure and has branched chains that cannot pack closely, so it is softer, more flexible and has a lower density (used for plastic bags and film). HDPE is made at lower temperature and pressure with a special catalyst; its chains are straighter and pack closely, so it is stronger, more rigid and has a higher density and softening point (used for bottles, buckets and pipes).

Thermosoftening polymers melt (soften) when they are heated, so they can be remoulded. They consist of individual, tangled polymer chains held together only by weak intermolecular forces. When heated, these forces are easily overcome so the chains can slide past each other. Examples include poly(ethene) and PVC.

Thermosetting polymers do not melt when they are heated; instead they char (decompose) at high temperatures. They have strong covalent cross-links between the polymer chains, which hold the chains rigidly in place. These cross-links are not broken by moderate heating. Thermosetting polymers are used for kettle handles, plug sockets and saucepan handles.

Most composites are made of two materials: a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the other material, which is called the reinforcement. Examples: fibreglass (glass fibres in a polymer resin matrix), carbon fibre composites (carbon fibres in resin), concrete (gravel and sand fragments in cement) and reinforced concrete (steel rods in concrete). Wood is a natural composite of cellulose fibres in a lignin matrix. The composite combines useful properties of both materials, for example the strength and low density of carbon fibre composites used in racing bikes and aircraft. You should be able to compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals, and explain how their properties relate to their uses.
keyFacts: Soda-lime glass: heat sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Borosilicate glass: sand and boron trioxide; melts at a higher temperature than soda-lime glass.
Clay ceramics (pottery, bricks): shape wet clay, then heat in a furnace.
Polymer properties depend on the monomers and the reaction conditions.
LDPE and HDPE are both made from ethene using different catalysts and conditions.
Thermosoftening polymers melt when heated: separate chains, weak intermolecular forces.
Thermosetting polymers do not melt when heated: covalent cross-links between chains.
Composites: a matrix (binder) surrounding fibres or fragments of a reinforcement.
Examples of composites: fibreglass, carbon fibre, concrete, reinforced concrete, wood.

keyTerms.definition: The most common glass, made by heating sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
Glass made from sand and boron trioxide that melts at a higher temperature than soda-lime glass.
A hard, brittle material such as pottery or brick, made by shaping wet clay and heating it in a furnace.
A polymer that melts or softens when heated; its chains are held by weak intermolecular forces.
A polymer that does not melt when heated because of covalent cross-links between chains.
A covalent bond joining one polymer chain to another.
A material made of two materials: a matrix (binder) surrounding a reinforcement of fibres or fragments.
The material in a composite that surrounds and binds together the reinforcement.

workedExamples.title: Comparing densities
workedExamples.question: A 50 cm³ block of a carbon fibre composite has a mass of 80 g. A 50 cm³ block of steel has a mass of 395 g. Calculate the density of each and how many times denser steel is.
workedExamples.answer: Composite 1.6 g/cm³; steel 7.9 g/cm³; steel is about 4.9 times denser.

workedExamples.title: Matching structure to behaviour on heating
workedExamples.question: Polymer X softens at 120 °C and can be remoulded. Polymer Y does not soften and chars at 300 °C. Identify each type and explain.
steps: X melts on heating, so it is thermosoftening.
Its chains are held by weak intermolecular forces, easily overcome by heating.
Y does not melt, so it is thermosetting: covalent cross-links hold the chains in place.
workedExamples.answer: X: thermosoftening (weak forces between chains). Y: thermosetting (cross-links).

workedExamples.title: Strength per mass
workedExamples.question: Material P has a tensile strength of 600 MPa and density 1.5 g/cm³. Material Q has a tensile strength of 400 MPa and density 7.8 g/cm³. Which has the greater strength per unit density?
steps: P has about 8 times the strength per unit density.
workedExamples.answer: P (for example a carbon fibre composite) is far stronger for its mass than Q (steel).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all glass is the same.
misconceptions.right: In fact soda-lime glass (sand, sodium carbonate, limestone) is most common, while borosilicate glass (sand, boron trioxide) melts at a higher temperature and is used for ovenware and lab glassware.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think thermosetting polymers melt at a higher temperature than thermosoftening ones.
misconceptions.right: In fact thermosetting polymers do not melt at all; they char or decompose because covalent cross-links hold the chains in place.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think LDPE and HDPE are made from different monomers.
misconceptions.right: In fact both are made from ethene; the different catalysts and reaction conditions give different chain structures and properties.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a composite is just any mixture of two materials.
misconceptions.right: In fact a composite has a matrix (binder) surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of a reinforcement.

realWorld: Pyrex measuring jugs and test tubes are made from borosilicate glass so they do not crack or soften when heated.
Reinforced concrete combines the compressive strength of concrete with the tensile strength of steel rods for bridges and buildings.
Carbon fibre composites are used in Formula 1 cars, tennis rackets and aircraft because they are strong and have low density.
Plug sockets are made from thermosetting polymers so they do not soften if they get hot.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only.
Soda-lime glass, borosilicate glass and clay ceramics: raw materials and how they are made.
Polymer properties depend on monomers and conditions: LDPE and HDPE from ethene.
Thermosoftening polymers (melt) versus thermosetting polymers (cross-links, do not melt).
Composites: matrix or binder plus reinforcement; compare properties of ceramics, polymers, composites and metals.
examTips: Learn the raw materials: soda-lime glass = sand + sodium carbonate + limestone; borosilicate = sand + boron trioxide.
For thermosoftening and thermosetting, always describe the structure (weak intermolecular forces versus cross-links) and the behaviour on heating.
Say 'intermolecular forces between chains' not 'bonds between chains' for thermosoftening polymers.
Name both parts of a composite: the matrix (binder) and the reinforcement (fibres or fragments).
In data questions, calculate density or strength per unit density and use it to justify the choice of material.
summary: Soda-lime glass: sand, sodium carbonate, limestone. Borosilicate: sand, boron trioxide, higher melting point.
Clay ceramics: shape wet clay, heat in a furnace.
Polymer properties depend on monomers and conditions (LDPE v HDPE).
Thermosoftening: weak forces between chains, melts. Thermosetting: cross-links, does not melt.
Composites: matrix or binder plus reinforcement.
Choose materials by comparing properties such as density, strength and melting point.

Shape wet clay, then heat it in a furnace.

flashcards.front: What do polymer properties depend on?
flashcards.back: The monomers they are made from and the conditions under which they are made.

flashcards.front: How do LDPE and HDPE differ in manufacture?
flashcards.back: Both from ethene, but different catalysts and reaction conditions.
Individual tangled chains held by weak intermolecular forces; melts when heated.
Chains joined by covalent cross-links; does not melt when heated.
A matrix (binder) surrounding and binding fibres or fragments of a reinforcement.
Glass fibres (reinforcement) in a polymer resin (matrix).
Sand and gravel fragments (reinforcement) in cement (binder).
Hard, brittle, high melting point, good insulators.

questions.question: Which raw materials are heated to make soda-lime glass?
markScheme: 1 mark: sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
questions.explanation: Sand and boron trioxide make borosilicate glass; clay makes ceramics.

questions.question: How are clay ceramics such as bricks made?
options: By shaping wet clay and then heating it in a furnace
markScheme: 1 mark: shaping wet clay and heating in a furnace
questions.explanation: Heating in a kiln hardens the shaped clay.

questions.question: Which of these is a composite material?
questions.explanation: Fibreglass is glass fibres in a polymer resin matrix. Brass is an alloy, which is not a composite.

questions.question: Why is borosilicate glass used for laboratory test tubes?
options: It is cheaper than soda-lime glass
It melts at a higher temperature than soda-lime glass
questions.explanation: Test tubes are heated strongly, so a glass with a higher melting point is needed.

questions.question: What is the same about LDPE and HDPE?
options: They are made using the same catalyst
They are both made from ethene
questions.explanation: Both are poly(ethene). Different catalysts and conditions give different properties, including density.

questions.question: What is the matrix in reinforced concrete?
questions.explanation: In reinforced concrete, the concrete is the matrix surrounding the steel rods, which are the reinforcement.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the structures of two polymers, A and B.
Polymer B is a thermosetting polymer.
Why does a thermosetting polymer not melt when heated?
options: Its chains are held only by weak intermolecular forces
It has covalent cross-links between the polymer chains
It has ionic bonds between chains
questions.explanation: Cross-links hold the chains rigidly in place. Weak intermolecular forces describe thermosoftening polymers.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the arrangement of polymer chains in LDPE and HDPE.
HDPE has a higher density than LDPE.
Which explanation is correct?
options: HDPE chains are straighter and pack more closely together
markScheme: 1 mark: straighter chains pack more closely
questions.explanation: Both contain only carbon and hydrogen; LDPE chains are branched and cannot pack closely. Neither has cross-links.

questions.question: Which material would be best for a plug socket that must not soften if it gets hot?
questions.explanation: Thermosetting polymers do not soften when heated and are good insulators. LDPE and PVC are thermosoftening; glass is brittle.

questions.question: Which property is typical of clay ceramics?
questions.explanation: Ceramics are hard, brittle, have high melting points and are insulators.

questions.question:
A piece of glass has a mass of 75 g and a volume of 30 cm³.
Calculate the density of the glass.
Use the equation:
density = mass ÷ volume
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume = 75 ÷ 30 = 2.5 g/cm³.

questions.question:
A bicycle frame can be made from steel or from a carbon fibre composite.
Both frames have a volume of 300 cm³.
Table 1 shows the density of each material.
Calculate the mass saved by using the carbon fibre composite instead of steel.
Use the equation:
mass = density × volume
markScheme: 1 mark: steel mass = 7.8 × 300 = 2340 g and composite mass = 1.6 × 300 = 480 g
questions.explanation: Mass = density × volume. The difference is (7.8 − 1.6) × 300 = 1860 g.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the masses of raw materials a glass maker mixes to make soda-lime glass.
Calculate the percentage by mass of sand in the mixture.

Table 1 shows data for two materials.
Calculate how many times greater the strength per unit density of the composite is than that of the aluminium alloy.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.explanation: Comparing strength per unit density shows why composites are used where low mass and high strength are both needed.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the densities of LDPE and HDPE.
Calculate the percentage by which the density of HDPE is greater than the density of LDPE.
questions.explanation: Difference = 0.04 g/cm³; 0.04 ÷ 0.92 × 100 = 4.35%. Always divide by the original (LDPE) value.

questions.question: Name the two raw materials used to make borosilicate glass.
questions.explanation: Borosilicate glass melts at a higher temperature than soda-lime glass.

questions.question: Name the two parts that make up most composite materials.
questions.explanation: The matrix surrounds and binds the reinforcement together.

questions.question: Give one example of a clay ceramic.
questions.explanation: Clay ceramics are made by shaping wet clay and heating it in a furnace.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the structures of two polymers, A and B.
Polymer A is a thermosoftening polymer.
Explain why thermosoftening polymers melt when heated.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are made of individual polymer chains (no cross-links)
1 mark: held together by weak intermolecular forces
1 mark: little energy is needed to overcome these forces, so chains can move/slide past each other
questions.explanation: Breaking intermolecular forces does not break the covalent bonds within the chains.

questions.question: State what the properties of a polymer depend on.
markScheme: 1 mark: the monomers it is made from
1 mark: the conditions under which it is made (for example catalyst, temperature, pressure)
questions.explanation: For example LDPE and HDPE are made from the same monomer under different conditions.

questions.question: Explain why HDPE rather than LDPE is used to make water pipes.
markScheme: 1 mark: HDPE is stronger / more rigid / has a higher softening point
1 mark: because its straighter chains pack more closely (stronger intermolecular forces)
questions.explanation: LDPE is too flexible and soft for pipes; it is better for bags and film.

questions.question: Wood is described as a natural composite. Use the definition of a composite to explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: wood is made of two materials
1 mark: cellulose fibres act as the reinforcement
1 mark: surrounded and bound together by a matrix (lignin)
questions.explanation: It fits the definition: a matrix binding together fibres of another material.

questions.question: Suggest why steel rods are put into concrete used for bridges.
markScheme: 1 mark: concrete is strong when squashed (compression) but weak and brittle when stretched or bent
1 mark: steel is strong in tension, so the composite combines the properties of both
questions.explanation: Reinforced concrete is a composite: concrete matrix, steel reinforcement.

questions.question: Compare the structure and properties of thermosoftening and thermosetting polymers, and give a use of each.
markScheme: Indicative content: thermosoftening: individual tangled chains, weak intermolecular forces, melt or soften on heating, can be remoulded and recycled, e.g. poly(ethene) bags or bottles; thermosetting: covalent cross-links between chains, do not melt on heating (char), rigid, e.g. kettle handles, plug sockets, saucepan handles.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of structure linked to behaviour on heating, with a suitable use for each.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example one melts and one does not.
questions.explanation: Link the structure (forces versus cross-links) to the behaviour when heated.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows properties of some materials.
Use the data to explain which material is most suitable for each of these uses:
• a window
• an oven tile
• a racing bicycle frame
• a drinks bottle.

rows: low strength; brittle; transparent; melts at about 700 °C

markScheme: Indicative content: (a) window: soda-lime glass, transparent, hard; brittle but acceptable; others opaque. (b) oven tile: clay ceramic, very high melting point (over 1500 °C), insulator, hard; HDPE would soften at 130 °C. (c) bicycle frame: carbon fibre composite, very strong with low density (1.6 v 7.8 g/cm³ for steel), not brittle, does not rust. (d) drinks bottle: HDPE, low density, flexible so does not shatter, can be moulded; glass is heavier and brittle.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): suitable choice for all four uses, each justified with relevant data and comparison with at least one alternative.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): suitable choices for most uses with some justification from the data.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two suitable choices with simple reasons.
questions.explanation: Quote numbers from the table and say why other materials are less suitable.

questions.question: Which monomer is used to make both LDPE and HDPE?
questions.explanation: LDPE and HDPE are both poly(ethene).

questions.question: A student says, 'Concrete is a composite because it is made from more than one substance.' Which is the best improvement to this explanation?
options: Concrete is a composite because it is hard
Concrete is a composite because it contains water
Concrete is a composite because cement acts as a binder surrounding fragments of sand and gravel
Concrete is a composite because it is a ceramic
questions.explanation: A composite needs a matrix (binder) and a reinforcement; being a mixture is not enough.
